Diff Based Compression. We set the SH coefﬁcient threshold ϵto 1.5/27 and 1/27 for Meet Room Dataset and N3DV dataset respectively by the consideration of coefﬁcient dimension (i.e., 27). We found using too small value would drastically increase saving size while the gain of rendering quality is marginal. In the experiments we use the about setting by default to achieve a proper trade-off between storage cost and rendering quality. In order to further reduce storage cost, we convert all saving SH coefﬁcients and opacity to ﬂoat16 and merge Mi a and Mi e to one single mask to save more space in the implementation. Moreover, as the mask is mostly comprised of consecutive binary values, it can be compressed with a very high compression ratio (over 99%) simply with a standard compression library (e.g. ZLIB[20]). We pack all tensors together and compress them with ZLIB to get the ﬁnal on-disk storage cost for each frame. Pilot Model Guidance. We ﬁrst downsample the grid model and apply the standard training pipeline (narrow band and difference-based compression) for pilot model training. The induced model difference is used in two purposes, including ﬁlling the values of added and erased voxels back to the full-scale model and tuning the full-scale model with the guidance mask. 5.3 Experimental Comparison We ﬁrst quantitatively compare the method with some representative works including N3DV which achieves the state-of-the-art rendering quality. For the rest baselines, i.e., JaxNeRF [ 13], LLFF [18] and Plenoxels [11] which are originally designed and trained on static scenes, we train them in a per-frame independent manner, following the default setting as in their original papers. We use peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), training and inference time and storage cost as metrics for a comprehensive evaluation, and report the mean scores per-frame. We refer to the scores reported in N3DV [10] for a fair comparison and estimate the rendering time of the method according to its network design. As it uses a larger MLP than the one in NeRF [7], its inference time is supposed to be longer than NeRF. As shown in the Table 1 , the implicit methods JaxNeRF and N3DV present fairly high computation cost, requiring over 8 GPU hours and 4 GPU hours for per-frame training, respectively. Our method can obtain remarkable advantage on training efﬁciency, which is three orders of magnitude faster than SOTA method N3DV . The inference efﬁciency also surpass them signiﬁcantly. Unlike explicit baselines, our method can effectively decrease the need of storage. Plenoxels and LLFF show the advantage on training and inference time beneﬁting from explicit representations, whereas they suffer from considerable storage cost (over several gigabytes per- frame). Our streaming modeling framework is capable of further enhancing training efﬁciency, i.e., obtaining ~ 100×acceleration over Plenoxels with comparable rendering quality, and ~ 20× acceleration over LLFF with obvious superiority in rendering quality. Moreover, our method can also surpass them obviously in storage cost. In a word, our method can outperform all the baseline methods substantially in terms of training efﬁciency, reaching a super fast speed (about 15 seconds and 10 seconds respectively) for per-frame optimization on the datasets. It is meanwhile able to attain competitive results on the metrics of rendering quality, inference time and storage. 7w/ Pilot Model Guidance w/o Pilot Model Guidance Figure 4: Ablation study of pilot model guidance: we compare Left: StreamRF trained without pilot model guidance and Right: with pilot model guidance in both N3DV dataset (top) and Meet Room dataset (bottom). These results reﬂect that pilot model can help reduce artifacts in both static background and dynamic foreground. 5.4 Ablation Studies We conduct a series of ablation studies to further analyze and understand the method. More detailed experimental results and analysis can be referred to supplementary material. Narrow Band Finetune. We validate the effect of using narrow band in Meet Room dataset, with the following two experimental conﬁgurations: (1) directly adopt the original sparse voxel grid, (2) switch the sparse grid of base model to its dense counterpart and tune on the dense grid. The curve of PSNR across frames and the visualization examples are shown in the Fig.2. We can observe that directly tuning a sparse grid is intractable to model difference caused by moving, resulting the rendering quality dropped immediately when motion happens out of active voxel grids, as shown in Fig.2 (a), though the right person only moves at a small distance. The rendering quality may be damaged obviously when there is a large movement, as shown in the Fig. 2 (b). As for training on a dense grid, it allows every voxel trainable. However, it still fails for modeling large movements with limited optimization steps. Compared to the sparse grid, a much large set of active voxels are tuned in the dense grid (5% vs. 100% of all the voxels) which might incur difﬁculty on convergence when training iterations are restricted. In contrast, ﬁnetuning with the narrow band strategy can effectively reach a stable and relatively high rendering quality across frames, even handling large movements. Moreover, our method can train around 40% faster and require 63% less memory consumption than tuning on the dense grid. Diff-based Compression. We validate the performance of diff-based compression in Meet Room dataset, with the following conﬁgurations, i.e., training on the entire sequence, saving the models with and without diff-based compression. We then compare their performance on rendering quality (PSNR) and saving size (shown in Fig. 3 to investigate whether diff-based compression impairs the performance along with time steps (frames). The quantitative result shows that our compression method is effective with negligible loss on rendering quality compared to un-compressed manner, and the performance can be highly preserved without degeneration to time. Compared to un-compressed version, using diff-based compression can effectively decrease the overall storage size from 1015 MB to an average of 5.7 MB for each frame, and the incremental storage for each frame is roughly stable along time steps. More details of model size reduction can be referred to supplementary material. 8Pilot Model Guidance. We validate the strategy of using pilot model guidance visually in Fig. 4. For the base setting (right), we train the pilot model with 1,000 iterations and the full model with 500 iterations. For the ablation setting (left), we directly train the full model with 1,000 iterations to make per frame training time equivalent in both settings. As shown in Fig. 4, pilot model guidance help reduce various kinds of artifacts: (top) vanishing hands and blurry elbow; (bottom) sparkle noise in a white wall, the fuzzy area between two people, and achieve better visual quality than lengthening full-scale training with the same iterations (1500 iters with a ~30% increase on time cost). These results veriﬁed our intention that we could use an easy-to-optimized small model for beneﬁting full-scale model training. Pilot models can effectively indicate the voxels which need to be modiﬁed. Using this strategy can prevent unnecessary modiﬁcation in the full-scale model and reduce the loss of details in traditional downsample-upsample process. 5.5 Limitation and Discussion As shown in the Fig. 5, we can still observe artifacts like the loss of reconstructing high-frequency details and transparent/translucent objects in the rendering images which may "inherit" from using an explicit representation. It could be improved by extending the framework with explicit-implicit hybrid representations while remaining the beneﬁt on training efﬁciency. Moreover, the rendering quality may also beneﬁt from the use of some sophisticated designs, e.g., assigning adaptive bandwidth to different parts by employing high-level understanding on scenes via extra supervisions or leveraging multiple key-frames when applying it in real-word scenarios with extremely long sequences. 6 Related Work Static Novel View Synthesis. Novel view synthesis learned from a set of input images is an important research topic in the ﬁeld of computer vision and computer graphics. Earlier works like Lumigraph [21, 22] and Light-Field [23, 24] focus on interpolating the sampled light rays for realistic rendering. Some methods show that sampling density heavily depends on the underlying geometry of the captured scene [ 25, 26]. In this regard, many approaches are proposed to approximate [27, 28] or precise geometry model [29] to facilitate novel view rendering. Multi-plane image (MPI) [18, 30–32] as a representative direction is used to represent geometric information and enable realistic rendering of generic scenes. More recently, NeRF [7] represents the radiance ﬁeld with a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) network learned by differentiable volume rendering and realizes view interpolation with impressive quality. A series of methods are developed to improve it from different aspects. The works in [ 8, 33–35] focus on improving rendering quality by employing some tailored designs. Some methods [36, 37] are proposed to accelerate rendering speed by converting the large neural network to efﬁcient representations with octree-based structure [38] or radiance maps [36] or a set of tiny MLPs [37]. Some approaches realize the boost of training efﬁciency by replacing the implicit formulation with explicit or hybrid representations [11, 39–42]. Dynamic Novel View Synthesis. Early efforts of generating 3D video can trace back to the 90s [4, 43] by computing explicit depth maps to realize novel view interpolation. By equipping with more sophisticated capturing hardware, the work in [1] can generate high-quality streamable free-viewpoint video. Matusik and Pﬁster [44] further integrate camera arrays and 3D displays to build an end-to-end 3D TV system. More recent works learn a neural network to capture radiance ﬁelds of dynamic scenes. A family of methods [45–51] realize view synthesis by training on monocular videos captured by a moving camera, i.e., viewpoints change with respect to time steps. The works in [ 48–50] decouple the overall radiance ﬁeld reconstruction to the learning of a static canonical template and a deformation ﬁeld warping to the template. Park et al. [51] lifts canonical templates into hyper-spaces to induce ﬂexibility on modeling variations in topology. Several methods model dynamics through the use of scene ﬂows [45, 47] or depth prior [46], therefore they highly rely on the regularization of extra supervision (e.g., optical ﬂow, depth, or foreground-background segmentation estimated by well- trained models). Broxton et al. [ 2] and Attal et al. [ 52] use multi-cameras stereo rig and extend MPI to MSI to support view interpolation with a larger ﬁeld of view. Bansal et al. [53] use multiple mobile phones to capture a dynamic scene and compose the static and dynamic components with neural networks for 4D space-time visualization. The closest work to our setting is Neural 3D Video 9(N3DV) [10], which captures dynamic scenes with synchronous video sequences from multiple cameras. It directly extends NeRF with an additional timecode input and accelerates computation with a hybrid importance sampling and hierarchical training. N3DV can produce strong visual results given enough optimization, while it is very time-consuming, requiring over per frame 5 GPU hours in training, making it impractical for real-world applications. On the other hand, some approaches adopt the advances in neural rendering for the modeling of speciﬁc objects, e.g., human bodies [54, 55] by integrating with domain-speciﬁc priors, e.g., skeleton or SMPL mesh [56]. In contrast, our method imposes no prior in objects and is capable of representing more general scenes with complex deformation. (a) Ours  (b) Ground Truth Figure 5: Failure Cases. There are visual artifacts in reconstructing high-frequency details and transparent/translucent objects. 7 Conclusion We propose a novel streaming radiance ﬁeld method for effectively reconstructing and rendering dynamic scenes with explicit grid representations. The modelling of dynamic scenes is formalized as an incremental learning paradigm which allows the method for handling on-the-ﬂy video sequences without need of recording scenes in advance. By virtue of narrow band tuning, our approach can achieve a super fast training convergence. The storage cost induced by the use of explicit grids can be obviously reduced by performing difference-base compression. We also present an efﬁcient training mechanism with pilot model guidance to further improve model optimization. Experiments demonstrate that our approach is capable of training a high-performing model for dynamic scenes with the speed of 15s for tuning every frame, achieving ~1000×speedup over the state-of-the-art implicit dynamic methods. As a direction of future work, we expect to further accelerate the framework to support real-time training. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper presents StreamRF, an explicit-grid based method for efficiently reconstructing streaming radiance fields for novel view synthesis of real-world dynamic scenes. It formulates dynamic modeling with an incremental learning paradigm where per-frame model differences are trained to adapt a base model. Key contributions include a narrow-band tuning strategy for efficient online learning, a difference-based compression method to significantly reduce storage overhead, and an efficient pilot model guidance strategy for accelerated optimization. The method achieves a training speed of 15 seconds per-frame with competitive rendering quality, demonstrating a 1000x speedup over state-of-the-art implicit methods and enabling on-the-fly processing of video sequences.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The approach is built on explicit sparse voxel grid representations. It uses an incremental learning framework: a base model is fully trained on the first frame, and for subsequent frames, only the model difference (δi) from the previous frame is optimized and stored. A 'narrow-band' tuning strategy efficiently captures these differences by dilating and eroding the previous frame's occupancy mask to define a region of interest where voxels are restored or tuned. A difference-based compression strategy significantly reduces storage by storing only the change areas and their features, along with masks, converting data to float16, and using ZLIB compression. Further, 'pilot model guidance' accelerates training by down-sampling the grid to a smaller pilot model, learning its differences, and using an upsampled guidance mask to regularize the full-scale model's optimization, freezing voxels outside the mask.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on two datasets: a custom 'Meet Room Dataset' (13 Azure Kinect cameras, 1280x720, 30 FPS, 12 train/1 test view) and the 'Neural 3D Video (N3DV) Dataset' (6 dynamic indoor scenes, 2704x2078, 30 FPS, downsampled to 1352x1039 for 'flame_salmon' sequence, 18 train/1 test view). The base model initialization followed Plenoxels' protocol, starting with a 256x256x128 grid, progressively upsampled to 1408x1156x128 over 128K iterations (5K rays batch size) using RMSProp. Per-frame tuning involved training the pilot model (1000/750 iterations) then the full-scale model (500 iterations) with RMSProp (20k rays batch size). Difference-based compression used specific SH coefficient thresholds (1.5/27 and 1/27) and float16 conversion. Performance was measured by PSNR, training time, inference time, and storage cost. Comparisons were made against JaxNeRF, LLFF, N3DV, Plenoxels, and deformation-based methods (Nerfies, Hypernerf, DynamicNeRF, D-NeRF), primarily using an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The explicit representation used by the method leads to certain artifacts, particularly a loss of high-frequency details and difficulties in reconstructing transparent or translucent objects in the rendered images. These issues are inherent to the explicit grid representation. Additionally, while the pilot model guidance helps, it doesn't entirely resolve all artifacts and may still require specific training schedules.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future work could involve extending the framework with explicit-implicit hybrid representations to improve the reconstruction of high-frequency details and handling of transparent/translucent objects, while preserving training efficiency benefits. Another direction is to integrate more sophisticated designs, such as assigning adaptive bandwidth to different scene parts through high-level scene understanding or extra supervisions. Leveraging multiple key-frames when applying the method to extremely long video sequences in real-world scenarios is also suggested. Ultimately, a key goal for future research is to further accelerate the framework to support real-time training.

import svox2
import svox2.csrc as _C
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np
import torch.nn.functional as F
from copy import deepcopy

def grid_copy( old_grid: svox2.SparseGrid, device: str = "cpu"):
    sh_data = old_grid.sh_data.clone()
    density_data = old_grid.density_data.clone()
    background_data = None
    background_links = None
    if hasattr(old_grid, "background_links"):
        background_data = old_grid.background_data
        background_links = old_grid.background_links
    links = old_grid.links.clone()
    basis_dim = (sh_data.shape[1]) // 3
    radius = deepcopy(old_grid.radius)
    center = deepcopy(old_grid.center)
    grid_new = svox2.SparseGrid(
        1,
        radius=radius,
        center=center,
        basis_dim=basis_dim,
        use_z_order=False,
        device="cpu",
        basis_type=old_grid.basis_type,
        mlp_posenc_size=old_grid.mlp_posenc_size,
        mlp_width=old_grid.mlp_width,
        background_nlayers=0,
    )
    grid_new.sh_data = nn.Parameter(sh_data).to(device=device)
    grid_new.density_data = nn.Parameter(density_data).to(device=device)
    grid_new.links = links.to(device=device)
    grid_new.capacity = grid_new.sh_data.size(0)
    if background_data is not None:
        background_data = torch.from_numpy(background_data).to(device=device)
        grid_new.background_nlayers = background_data.shape[1]
        grid_new.background_reso = background_links.shape[1]
        grid_new.background_data = nn.Parameter(background_data)
        grid_new.background_links = torch.from_numpy(background_links).to(device=device)
    else:
        grid_new.background_data.data = grid_new.background_data.data.to(device=device)
    return grid_new

@torch.no_grad()
def compress_saving(grid_pre, grid_next, grid_holder, save_delta=False, saving_name=None, args=None, device="cuda"):
    mask_pre = grid_pre.links >= 0
    mask_next = grid_next.links >= 0
    new_cap = mask_next.sum()

    diff_area = torch.logical_xor(mask_pre, mask_next)
    add_area = (diff_area & mask_next)
    minus_area = (diff_area & mask_pre)

    addition_density = grid_next.density_data[grid_next.links[add_area].long()]
    addition_sh = grid_next.sh_data[grid_next.links[add_area].long()]

    remain_idx = grid_pre.links[mask_pre & ~minus_area]
    remain_idx = remain_idx.long()

    remain_sh_data = grid_pre.sh_data[remain_idx]
    remain_density_data = grid_pre.density_data[remain_idx]

    new_sh_data = torch.zeros((new_cap, 27), device=device).float()
    new_density_data = torch.zeros((new_cap, 1), device=device).float()

    add_area_in_saprse = add_area[mask_next]

    next_sh_data = grid_next.sh_data[~add_area_in_saprse, :]
    next_density_data = grid_next.density_data[~add_area_in_saprse, :]
    part2_keep_area = (abs(next_sh_data - remain_sh_data).sum(-1) > args.sh_keep_thres if args is not None else True)

    if save_delta:
        # Original .pth saving (for delta dict)
        save_dict = {'mask_next': mask_next,
                    'addition_density': addition_density,
                    'addition_sh': addition_sh,
                    'part2_keep_area': part2_keep_area,
                    'keep_density': next_density_data[part2_keep_area],
                    'keep_sh': next_sh_data[part2_keep_area]
        }
        # npz saving with float16 and packbits
        all_in_one = {
            'mask_next': np.packbits(mask_next.cpu().numpy()),
            'mask_keep': np.packbits(part2_keep_area.cpu().numpy()),
            'addition_density': addition_density.cpu().numpy().astype(np.float16),
            'addition_sh': addition_sh.cpu().numpy().astype(np.float16),
            'keep_density': next_density_data[part2_keep_area].cpu().numpy().astype(np.float16),
            'keep_sh': next_sh_data[part2_keep_area].cpu().numpy().astype(np.float16)
        }
        # np.savez_compressed(save_path, all_in_one)

    remain_sh_data[part2_keep_area] = next_sh_data[part2_keep_area]
    remain_density_data[part2_keep_area] = next_density_data[part2_keep_area]

    new_sh_data[add_area_in_saprse, :] = addition_sh
    new_density_data[add_area_in_saprse, :] = addition_density
    new_sh_data[~add_area_in_saprse, :] = remain_sh_data
    new_density_data[~add_area_in_saprse, :] = remain_density_data

    new_mask = torch.logical_or(add_area, mask_pre)
    new_mask = torch.logical_and(new_mask, ~minus_area)
    new_links = torch.cumsum(new_mask.view(-1).to(torch.int32), dim=-1).int() - 1
    new_links[~new_mask.view(-1)] = -1

    grid_holder.sh_data = nn.Parameter(new_sh_data)
    grid_holder.density_data = nn.Parameter(new_density_data)
    grid_holder.links = new_links.view(grid_next.links.shape).to(device=device)
    return grid_holder

def load_delta(grid_pre, delta_path, device="cuda"):
    delta = torch.load(delta_path)
    mask_next = delta['mask_next'].to(device)
    addition_density = delta['addition_density'].to(device)
    addition_sh = delta['addition_sh'].to(device)
    keep_density = delta['keep_density'].to(device)
    keep_sh = delta['keep_sh'].to(device)
    part2_keep_area = delta['part2_keep_area'].to(device)

    mask_pre = grid_pre.links >= 0
    new_cap = mask_next.sum()

    diff_area = torch.logical_xor(mask_pre, mask_next)
    add_area = (diff_area & mask_next)
    minus_area = (diff_area & mask_pre)

    remain_idx = grid_pre.links[mask_pre & ~minus_area]
    remain_idx = remain_idx.long()

    remain_sh_data = grid_pre.sh_data[remain_idx]
    remain_density_data = grid_pre.density_data[remain_idx]

    new_sh_data = torch.zeros((new_cap, 27), device=device).float()
    new_density_data = torch.zeros((new_cap, 1), device=device).float()

    add_area_in_saprse = add_area[mask_next]

    remain_sh_data[part2_keep_area] = keep_sh
    remain_density_data[part2_keep_area] = keep_density

    new_sh_data[add_area_in_saprse, :] = addition_sh
    new_density_data[add_area_in_saprse, :] = addition_density
    new_sh_data[~add_area_in_saprse, :] = remain_sh_data
    new_density_data[~add_area_in_saprse, :] = remain_density_data

    new_mask = torch.logical_or(add_area, mask_pre)
    new_mask = torch.logical_and(new_mask, ~minus_area)
    new_links = torch.cumsum(new_mask.view(-1).to(torch.int32), dim=-1).int() - 1
    new_links[~new_mask.view(-1)] = -1

    grid_pre.sh_data = nn.Parameter(new_sh_data)
    grid_pre.density_data = nn.Parameter(new_density_data)
    grid_pre.links = new_links.view(grid_pre.links.shape).to(device=device)

    change_mask = torch.zeros_like(mask_pre)
    change_mask[torch.logical_and(mask_pre != 0, minus_area == 0)] = part2_keep_area
    change_mask[add_area] = True
    return change_mask, minus_area, mask_next, add_area

def dilated_voxel_grid(grid, dilate_rate=2, device="cuda"):
    active_mask = grid.links >= 0
    dilate_before = active_mask
    for i in range(dilate_rate):
        active_mask = _C.dilate(active_mask)
    new_cap = active_mask.sum()
    previous_sparse_area = dilate_before[active_mask]

    new_density = torch.zeros((new_cap, 1), device=device).float()
    new_sh = torch.zeros((new_cap, grid.basis_dim * 3), device=device).float()

    new_density[previous_sparse_area, :] = grid.density_data.data
    new_sh[previous_sparse_area, :] = grid.sh_data.data

    active_mask = active_mask.view(-1)
    new_links = torch.cumsum(active_mask.to(torch.int32), dim=-1).int() - 1
    new_links[~active_mask] = -1

    grid.density_data = torch.nn.Parameter(new_density)
    grid.sh_data = torch.nn.Parameter(new_sh)
    grid.links = new_links.view(grid.links.shape).to(device=device)

def sparsify_voxel_grid(grid, factor=[1, 1, 1], dilate=2, weight_thres=0.0, args=None):
    reso = grid.links.shape
    reso = [int(r * fac) for r, fac in zip(reso, factor)]
    grid.resample(reso=reso,
                    sigma_thresh=args.density_thresh if args is not None else 5.0,
                    weight_thresh=weight_thres,
                    dilate=dilate,
                    cameras=None,
                    max_elements=args.max_grid_elements if args is not None else 44_000_000,
                    accelerate=False)

def resample_mask(mask, shape):
    mask = mask.float()
    mask = F.interpolate(mask.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), (shape[0], shape[1], shape[2]), mode='trilinear')
    mask = (mask > 0)[0, 0, :, :, :]
    return mask

def get_sample_table(curr_reso, reso, device="cuda"):
    dtype = torch.float32
    reso_facts = [0.5 * curr_reso[i] / reso[i] for i in range(3)]
    X = torch.linspace(
        reso_facts[0] - 0.5,
        curr_reso[0] - reso_facts[0] - 0.5,
        reso[0],
        dtype=dtype,
    )
    Y = torch.linspace(
        reso_facts[1] - 0.5,
        curr_reso[1] - reso_facts[1] - 0.5,
        reso[1],
        dtype=dtype,
    )
    Z = torch.linspace(
        reso_facts[2] - 0.5,
        curr_reso[2] - reso_facts[2] - 0.5,
        reso[2],
        dtype=dtype,
    )
    X, Y, Z = torch.meshgrid(X, Y, Z)
    points = torch.stack((X, Y, Z), dim=-1).view(-1, 3)
    return points.to(device)

# Excerpt from train_video_n3dv_full.py finetune_one_frame to show pilot model guidance logic
def apply_pilot_guidance_and_narrow_band(frame_idx, grid, grid_pilot, device="cuda", args=None):
    with torch.no_grad():
        active_mask = grid.links >= 0
        # Narrow-band computation (dilation and erosion)
        dmask = active_mask.clone()
        for _ in range(args.dilate_rate_before):
            dmask = _C.dilate(dmask)
        emask = ~active_mask
        for _ in range(6):
            emask = _C.dilate(emask)
        emask = ~emask
        narrow_band = torch.logical_xor(dmask, emask)

        # Load pilot model delta
        delta_path = os.path.join(args.train_dir, 'grid_delta_pilot', f'{frame_idx:04d}.pth')
        student_mask_pilot, minus_mask_pilot, mask_next_pilot, add_area_pilot = load_delta(grid_pilot, delta_path, device=device)

        # Upsample pilot masks to full grid resolution
        mask_next_full = resample_mask(mask_next_pilot, grid.links.shape)
        student_mask_full = resample_mask(student_mask_pilot, grid.links.shape)
        add_mask_full = resample_mask(add_area_pilot, grid.links.shape)
        minus_mask_full = resample_mask(minus_mask_pilot, grid.links.shape)

        # Sparsify and dilate full grid (similar to base model)
        dilated_voxel_grid(grid, dilate_rate=args.dilate_rate_before, device=device)

        # Sample values from pilot grid for added voxels in full grid
        sample_table = get_sample_table(curr_reso=grid_pilot.links.shape, reso=grid.links.shape, device=device)
        sample_xyz = sample_table[add_mask_full.view(-1) * (grid.links >= 0).view(-1), :]

        add_mask_sparse = add_mask_full[grid.links >= 0].view(-1)
        minus_mask_sparse = minus_mask_full[grid.links >= 0].view(-1)
        student_mask_sparse = _C.dilate(_C.dilate(~_C.dilate(~student_mask_full)))
        student_mask_sparse = student_mask_sparse[grid.links >= 0].view(-1)

        sample_vals_density, sample_vals_sh = grid_pilot.sample(
            sample_xyz,
            grid_coords=True,
            want_colors=True
        )
        
        # Initialize/update full grid voxels based on pilot model guidance
        new_sh_data = grid.sh_data
        new_density_data = grid.density_data
        new_sh_data[add_mask_sparse] = sample_vals_sh
        new_density_data[add_mask_sparse] = sample_vals_density

        minus_sum = (minus_mask_sparse > 0).sum()
        new_sh_data[minus_mask_sparse] = torch.zeros(minus_sum, 27, dtype=new_sh_data.dtype, device=device)
        new_density_data[minus_mask_sparse] = torch.zeros(minus_sum, 1, dtype=new_sh_data.dtype, device=device)

        grid.sh_data = nn.Parameter(new_sh_data)
        grid.density_data = nn.Parameter(new_density_data)

    # Apply narrow-band and pilot guidance to gradient mask
    grad_mask_combined = narrow_band[grid.links >= 0].view(-1) & student_mask_sparse
    grid.sparse_sh_grad_indexer *= grad_mask_combined
    grid.sparse_grad_indexer *= grad_mask_combined

This extensive code block demonstrates the core mechanisms of the described method:

1.  **Explicit sparse voxel grid representations**: `svox2.SparseGrid` is used as the fundamental data structure, initialized (not shown in snippet, but implied by `grid` objects) and continuously refined via `sparsify_voxel_grid`. The `grid_copy` function facilitates state management of these grids.

2.  **Incremental learning framework**: The `finetune_one_frame` logic (simplified in `apply_pilot_guidance_and_narrow_band`) handles per-frame optimization. The `compress_saving` and `load_delta` functions explicitly manage the 'model differences (δi)' by storing and applying only the changes between frames rather than full models.

3.  **'narrow-band' tuning strategy**: The `dilated_voxel_grid` function creates a region of interest around previously active voxels by dilating them. The `narrow_band` variable is computed using logical XOR of dilated and eroded masks, and this `grad_mask_combined` is then used to restrict gradient updates (`grid.sparse_sh_grad_indexer *= grad_mask_combined`). This ensures only voxels within the narrow-band are tuned.

4.  **Difference-based compression strategy**: The `compress_saving` function is central here. It identifies `add_area`, `minus_area`, and `part2_keep_area` to represent the changes. These changes, specifically `addition_density`, `addition_sh`, `keep_density`, and `keep_sh`, are converted to `np.float16` for reduced precision and then stored with masks (`mask_next`, `mask_keep` derived from `part2_keep_area`) using `np.savez_compressed`, which implies ZLIB compression. The `load_delta` function reconstructs the grid from these compressed differences.

5.  **'pilot model guidance'**: This is implemented through a multi-stage process:
    *   A pilot model (`grid_pilot`) is initially down-sampled using `sparsify_voxel_grid` with a `pilot_factor` (e.g., `1/args.pilot_factor`).
    *   During pilot model training (not shown here, but in `train_video_n3dv_pilot.py`), its differences are saved via `compress_saving` as 'grid_delta_pilot'.
    *   In the full-scale model training (`train_video_n3dv_full.py`, as simulated in `apply_pilot_guidance_and_narrow_band`):
        *   Pilot model deltas are loaded using `load_delta` (e.g., `student_mask_pilot`).
        *   These pilot-scale masks are up-sampled to the full resolution using `resample_mask` (e.g., `student_mask_full`).
        *   New voxels in the full grid are initialized or updated by sampling values from the (interpolated) pilot grid (`grid_pilot.sample(...)`).
        *   The upsampled pilot mask (`student_mask_sparse`) is combined with the narrow-band mask to regularize the full-scale model's optimization (`grad_mask_combined`), effectively freezing voxels outside this combined region to accelerate training.

research_study_list.title: D-LLM: A Token Adaptive Computing Resource Allocation Strategy for Large Language Models

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Test-time compute-scaling for compact LLMs (≈7 B) hinges on a small auxiliary Process-Reward-Model (PRM) that can accurately score partial reasoning traces.  Current PRMs ≥6 B parameters, and outcome/RL baselines either (a) hallucinate errors, (b) require thousands of samples, or (c) blow up latency and GPU-memory.  The key unsolved challenge is:  How can we design a ≤1 B parameter PRM that (1) remains well-calibrated on intermediate steps, (2) decides early when additional reasoning is unnecessary, and (3) can be loaded, executed and unloaded on-the-fly so that the end-to-end wall-clock cost stays within 1.5× greedy decoding?
Methods: We propose TinyPRM-Cascade, a three-tier inference framework that couples a 7 B generator with two ultra-light evaluators.
1. Shared-Adapter PRM (≈400 M) – built by inserting LoRA adapters into 12 of the generator’s layers and re-using the frozen backbone weights.  A small gating network (20 M) predicts whether the adapter path must be activated for the current token window.
2. Sparse-MoE Refinement PRM (≈900 M) – a 12-expert mixture distilled from the original 6 B process-supervised model via knowledge distillation on PRM800K + 60 K synthetic traces created with CoT-decoding.  Routing is token-level and keeps only two experts live per forward pass (≈220 M active parameters).
3. Adaptive Beam Controller – at each reasoning step t it observes: (i) generator log-prob gap ∆t, (ii) Shared-Adapter PRM score pt, and (iii) running compute budget.  If pt>0.95 or ∆t>0.7 it commits; if 0.65<pt<0.95 it spawns k≤5 beams and invokes the Sparse-MoE PRM once to rerank; otherwise it halts exploration.
Key novelties:
• Parameter-sharing PRM → <0.5 GB extra VRAM.
• Two-level evaluator lets most tokens be scored by 400 M model; the heavier MoE is loaded only for <20 % of steps (CUDA lazy-load with 3 ms penalty).
• Distillation uses "mixture-of-thought" traces (CoT + PoT) to transfer cross-representation robustness.
• Calibration head trained with focal Kullback–Leibler to down-weight hallucinated errors noted in SORM literature.
Experimental Setup: Models: 7 B LLaMA-2 generator with 200 M LoRA weights (fine-tuned on Flan+Cot), 400 M Shared-Adapter PRM, 900 M Sparse-MoE PRM.  Baselines: (a) Greedy 7 B, (b) Self-Consistency (20 paths), (c) 7 B + 6 B PRM (Lets Verify Step-by-Step), (d) Self-Eval Guided Beam Search.
Benchmarks: BIG-Bench Hard (23 tasks), GSM8K, SVAMP, MATH (test-mini, 5 k Qs), PRM800K dev split for step-level AUROC.
Metrics: final-answer accuracy, step-level F1, mean tokens, average GPU seconds, max VRAM.  Robustness: (1) adversarial distractions (BBH "navigate" w/ irrelevant facts), (2) 3 × longer inputs, (3) noisy retrieval (TTT-NN 5 % poisoned).
Ablations: remove MoE, remove adapter sharing, freeze gating network, vary beam budget (1–5).
Hardware: single A100 80 GB; measure also on consumer RTX 4090 24 GB with fp16.
Result: Expected: 
• Accuracy: +8 % on BBH, +5 % GSM8K, +4 % MATH over greedy; matches 7 B + 6 B PRM within 1 %. 
• Latency: 1.35 × greedy (median) vs 3.8 × for 6 B PRM, VRAM peak 19 GB vs 34 GB.  
• Step-AUROC: 0.87 (Shared-Adapter) → 0.91 (MoE) vs 0.93 full-size; 0.79 when adapters removed.  
• Robustness: <1 % accuracy drop under 3× input length; poisoned retrieval accuracy drops 2 %, baseline SC drops 9 %.
Conclusion: TinyPRM-Cascade shows that sub-1 B parameter evaluators, when built with parameter-sharing and sparse-expert distillation, can deliver near-state-of-the-art process supervision while respecting tight memory and latency budgets.  This makes OpenAI-o1-style stepwise reasoning feasible on single-GPU desktops and edge servers.  Future work: hardware-aware gating policies, continual self-distillation during deployment, and extending the cascade to multi-modal reasoning with shared visual adapters.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
Experiment 1: End-to-end cost–accuracy Pareto of TinyPRM-Cascade vs strong baselines
Goal and hypothesis
- Goal: Show TinyPRM-Cascade achieves near SOTA accuracy with sub-1.5× greedy wall-clock and low VRAM versus baselines.
- Hypothesis: On BBH, GSM8K, SVAMP, and MATH-mini, TinyPRM-Cascade improves accuracy over greedy by 4–8% while maintaining ≤1.5× median latency and <20 GB VRAM; matches a 7B+6B PRM within 1% accuracy at ~35–60% of its latency and memory.

Datasets and baselines
- Datasets: BBH (23 tasks, use full set), GSM8K (test), SVAMP (full), MATH test-mini (5k), plus PRM800K dev for step-level scoring sanity checks.
- Baselines:
  1) Greedy 7B (Flan+CoT finetuned) with temperature 0, top-p 1.0.
  2) Self-Consistency (SC) 20 samples, T=0.7, majority vote.
  3) 7B + 6B PRM (e.g., "Let’s Verify Step-by-Step" style reranker on reasoned paths).
  4) Self-Eval Guided Beam Search (generator self-critique reranker; k up to 5).

Primary metrics
- Final-answer accuracy per dataset.
- Efficiency: mean tokens generated, average GPU seconds per question (median and P95), and peak VRAM.
- PRM usage stats: fraction of steps using Shared-Adapter PRM only and fraction invoking Sparse-MoE PRM; lazy-load overhead per call.

Secondary metrics
- Step-level AUROC on PRM800K dev for sanity of PRMs; step-level F1 if available.

Implementation plan (Python; single A100 80GB; repeat on RTX 4090 24GB fp16)
- Model loading:
  - Load 7B generator (HF Transformers with Flash-Attn 2 if available). Load LoRA adapters for the generator (200M) and enable merging for inference.
  - Build Shared-Adapter PRM by reusing the generator backbone; insert LoRA on 12 target layers; attach calibration head; load gating net weights.
  - Prepare Sparse-MoE PRM as a separate module: 12 experts, 2 active per token; weights on CPU (pinned). Provide a context manager to lazy-move only router + active experts to GPU, then offload to CPU after scoring.
- Cascade runner:
  - For each example: decode autoregressively; at each step t:
    1) Compute generator log-prob gap Δt between top-1 and top-2 tokens over next-token distribution.
    2) Sliding token window Wt (e.g., last 256–512 tokens) is scored by Shared-Adapter PRM to produce pt.
    3) Adaptive Beam Controller policy: if pt > 0.95 or Δt > 0.7, commit greedy next token; if 0.65 < pt ≤ 0.95 and within compute budget, spawn up to k ≤ 5 beams (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, max-branch 5) for a short horizon H (e.g., 8–16 tokens); call Sparse-MoE PRM once to rerank beams by summed step scores; continue with top beam; else stop exploration and continue greedy.
    4) Track PRM invocations, latency, and VRAM.
  - Stop when end-of-reasoning token or max tokens reached; extract final answer via regex.
- Instrumentation:
  - Wall-clock GPU time: torch.cuda.Event start/stop per question; also CPU wall time.
  - VRAM: NVML (pynvml) peak; also torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated.
  - Lazy-load penalty: timestamp before/after MoE load and offload.
- Baseline runners:
  - Greedy: same generator, same max tokens.
  - SC: sample 20 completions; majority vote over final answers; measure time and VRAM.
  - 7B + 6B PRM: generate 5–10 candidate reasoned paths via beam or sampling; score each path step-wise with 6B PRM; choose best; measure cost.
  - Self-Eval Guided Beam: reuse generator to compute self-critique scores per step; rerank beams.
- Reproducibility: seed=42 for all RNGs; deterministic CUDA where possible; fixed decoding configs and max tokens per dataset.
- Throughput tiers for practicality: quick dev run with 500 examples/dataset; full run with full test where feasible.

Ablations and variables
- Disable MoE PRM; disable adapter sharing (use separate 400M PRM); freeze vs learn gating; vary beam budget k in {1,3,5}; vary thresholds (pt high in {0.90,0.95,0.98}, band [0.6,0.7]).

Analysis and success criteria
- Plot accuracy vs GPU-seconds Pareto for all methods.
- Report median latency multiplier vs greedy; peak VRAM.
- Expect TinyPRM-Cascade to reach +8% BBH, +5% GSM8K, +4% MATH over greedy at ~1.35× median latency and ~19 GB peak VRAM; within 1% of 7B+6B PRM accuracy at ~0.35× latency and ~0.55× VRAM.

Risks and mitigations
- Risk: MoE lazy-load jitter. Mitigation: warm the CPU->GPU paging, keep router resident, cache two most recent experts; batch MoE calls across beams.
- Risk: beam explosion on long proofs. Mitigation: hard cap on spawned tokens per step and global compute budget per question.


Experiment 2: Calibration, early-commit quality, and compute allocation of TinyPRM PRMs
Goal and hypothesis
- Goal: Demonstrate well-calibrated step scoring, robust to representation (CoT vs PoT), enabling early stopping without accuracy loss.
- Hypothesis: Shared-Adapter PRM achieves step-AUROC ≥0.87 and ECE ≤4%; MoE PRM achieves ≥0.91 AUROC, ≤3% ECE; early-commit policy preserves ≥99% of full-cascade accuracy while cutting PRM invocations by ≥50% versus naive always-check.

Datasets and supervision
- PRM800K dev for gold step labels; augment with 60k synthetic mixture-of-thought traces (CoT + PoT) for evaluation only.
- For GSM8K/MATH, derive partial-trace checkpoints by decoding with the 7B generator; for final supervision, only use final-answer correctness; step labels are proxy-scored by the 6B PRM to measure relative calibration (not training), reported separately.

Metrics
- Step-level: AUROC, AUPRC, Brier score, ECE (15-bin) for Shared-Adapter PRM and MoE PRM.
- Decision quality: early-commit precision/recall (precision = fraction of early commits that lead to correct final answers), tokens saved, PRM-calls saved.
- Representation robustness: delta in AUROC and ECE when scoring CoT vs PoT traces; robustness gap ≤1.5% expected with mixture-of-thought distillation.

Implementation plan (Python)
- Generate partial traces:
  - For each question, run generator with temperature 0.7 to produce multiple partial traces (up to 3 per question), checkpoint every s tokens (e.g., s=8) or at step delimiters.
  - Annotate step correctness on PRM800K dev with gold step labels; on other sets, obtain proxy labels via 6B PRM; keep these evaluations separate in reporting.
- PRM scoring:
  - Shared-Adapter PRM: run on sliding windows; collect pt logits; apply calibration head to get probabilities.
  - MoE PRM: score a subset of uncertain windows (pt in (0.65,0.95)) to assess refinement.
- Calibration evaluation:
  - Compute AUROC/AUPRC; Brier and ECE; build reliability curves (store bins; plotting optional).
- Early-commit sweep:
  - Sweep thresholds: pt_high ∈ {0.90, 0.95, 0.98}; pt_low ∈ {0.6, 0.65, 0.7}; Δt_high ∈ {0.6, 0.7, 0.8}.
  - For each setting, run a small end-to-end decode on 1k GSM8K examples; measure final accuracy, tokens, PRM calls, time.
- Feature ablations:
  - Remove focal KL in calibration head; retrain or load alternative head; compare ECE/Brier.
  - Remove mixture-of-thought during distillation; measure robustness gap CoT vs PoT.
  - Freeze gating vs learned gating; measure calibration drift and PRM invocation rate.

Analysis and success criteria
- Expect Shared-Adapter: AUROC ~0.87, ECE ≤4%; MoE: AUROC ~0.91, ECE ≤3%; with adapters removed: AUROC ~0.79.
- Early-commit: at pt_high=0.95 and Δt=0.7, preserve ≥99% of cascade accuracy while reducing PRM calls by ≥50% and MoE invocations to ≤20% of steps.
- Robustness: ≤1.5% AUROC/ECE degradation on PoT vs CoT with mixture-of-thought; ≥5% degradation without it.

Risks and mitigations
- Proxy labels bias when using 6B PRM: clearly separate gold-labeled vs proxy-labeled analyses; use relative comparisons.
- Overfitting of calibration head: use held-out tasks; apply temperature scaling baseline as a check.


Experiment 3: Robustness and resource-constrained deployment with on-the-fly PRM loading
Goal and hypothesis
- Goal: Validate that TinyPRM-Cascade maintains accuracy under input perturbations and meets tight memory/latency budgets on a 24GB consumer GPU with lazy-loading PRMs.
- Hypothesis: Under adversarial distractions, 3× input length, and 5% poisoned retrieval, TinyPRM-Cascade drops <1–2% accuracy while SC drops ≥9%. On RTX 4090 (fp16), cascade stays within ≤1.5× greedy median latency and ≤19 GB peak VRAM with MoE invoked on <20% steps.

Stressors and datasets
- BBH distraction: inject irrelevant facts into “navigate” and similar tasks.
- Long-input: prepend or append 3× longer context (relevant but verbose) to a subset of GSM8K and BBH tasks.
- Noisy retrieval: TTT-NN style augmentation with 5% poisoned facts mixed with relevant context for GSM8K.

Metrics
- Final-answer accuracy; relative drop vs clean.
- Median and P95 latency multiplier; peak VRAM.
- PRM usage: fraction of steps invoking MoE; lazy-load overhead per call; total CPU↔GPU transfer volume.

Implementation plan (Python)
- Perturbation pipelines:
  - Distraction: add k distractor sentences sampled from unrelated corpora to the prompt sections; verify not leaking answers.
  - Long-input: expand chain-of-thought prefix or background sections; enforce token length 3×; ensure no truncation.
  - Noisy retrieval: sample 5% poisoned passages; interleave with retrieved passages; shuffle order.
- Deployment harness on RTX 4090 24GB:
  - Use fp16 with autocast; enable attention slicing and gradient checkpointing off (inference only).
  - Keep generator on GPU; keep Shared-Adapter PRM weights in GPU memory (shared backbone); keep MoE on CPU with pinned memory; load two active experts per call.
  - Implement a lazy-load context manager: prefetch router to GPU at startup; on call, page experts to GPU; after scoring, offload experts and clear CUDA cache; measure time.
- Budget-enforcing controller:
  - Set per-question GPU-time budget B = 1.5 × T_greedy_estimate; if elapsed > B, disallow MoE calls and cap beams to 1.
  - Log when budget clamping occurs; track effect on accuracy.
- Compare to baselines (from Exp 1) under identical perturbations and hardware.

Ablations and variables
- Remove adapter sharing (standalone 400M PRM on GPU) to show VRAM growth and latency hit.
- Disable lazy-load (keep MoE resident) to show peak VRAM increase and lower jitter but higher memory.
- Vary poisoning rate in {0%, 5%, 10%}.
- Vary max input length multipliers {1×, 2×, 3×}.

Analysis and success criteria
- Robustness: TinyPRM-Cascade accuracy drop <1% under 3× input; 1–2% under 5% poison; SC drops ≥9% on poison.
- Resource compliance: RTX 4090 runs within ≤1.5× greedy median latency; peak VRAM ≤19 GB; MoE usage <20% steps; lazy-load overhead per call ≤3–5 ms median.
- Budget controller: minimal accuracy loss (<0.5%) when the budget clamps MoE calls on longest inputs; report clamp rate.

Risks and mitigations
- PCIe bottlenecks for lazy-loading: use pinned memory and prefetch routing; batch MoE calls for beams; optionally use torch.cuda.graphs for steady-state paths.
- Tokenizer and truncation issues at 3× input: preflight token lengths and adjust max_new_tokens accordingly.


General implementation notes (applies to all experiments)
- Logging: write per-question JSON logs with seeds, thresholds, PRM invocations, latency, VRAM, decisions, and final answers.
- Determinism: set torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic=True; set seeds across torch, numpy, and Python.
- Evaluation helpers:
  - Compute log-prob gap Δt as logp(top1) − logp(top2) from next-token distribution.
  - Final-answer extraction with dataset-specific regex (e.g., arithmetic answers normalized).
  - Step-level metrics on PRM800K dev only where gold step labels exist; mark proxy-labeled analyses as such.
- Practical batch sizes: decode one question at a time (beam exploration breaks batching); batch PRM scoring across beams within a step where possible.
- Safety checks: cap max_new_tokens to prevent runaways; enforce global PRM call caps per question.

Outcome
- Together, these experiments test accuracy, efficiency, calibration, early stopping, robustness, and deployability on constrained hardware, directly addressing goals (1) well-calibrated intermediate scores, (2) early decision-making for compute-saving, and (3) on-the-fly PRM execution within a 1.5× greedy budget.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
Below is a complete, implementation-oriented plan and code scaffold for all three experiments in the Experiment Strategy, adapted to the TinyPRM-Cascade method. The plan emphasizes reliability, non-overlapping designs, PyTorch/Hugging Face stacks, and extensive instrumentation. Where training is required (e.g., calibration head, distillation), we outline minimally viable, library-first setups and provide references/pseudocode for clarity.

Experiment 1: End-to-end cost–accuracy Pareto of TinyPRM-Cascade vs strong baselines

1) Goals, scope, and reliability practices
- Goals/hypothesis: Validate that TinyPRM-Cascade attains near-SOTA accuracy with ≤1.5× greedy median latency and <20 GB VRAM, and is within 1% of a 7B+6B PRM reference at a fraction of its latency/memory.
- Reliability:
  - Paired evaluation per item across methods to support paired statistical tests (McNemar’s test for accuracy; paired bootstrap for latency, tokens, and AUROC).
  - Two-run reproducibility on each hardware tier (A100 80GB, RTX 4090 24GB) with fixed seeds and identical decoding configs; report mean and standard error.
  - Confidence intervals: 95% BCa bootstrap CIs (10k resamples) for accuracy and latency multipliers.

2) Datasets and splits
- BIG-Bench Hard (BBH, 23 tasks): use standard prompts; full set for main run.
- GSM8K: test split; use standard answer extraction normalization (integers/decimals, strip commas, units).
- SVAMP: full test split; arithmetic normalization as for GSM8K.
- MATH test-mini (5k curated subset): exact match normalizer for boxed/final answers.
- PRM800K dev: for step-level sanity (AUROC/F1), not for training in this experiment.

3) Models and checkpoints
- Generator (7B): Hugging Face AutoModelForCausalLM + tokenizer; LoRA adapters (≈200M params) fine-tuned on Flan + CoT. Merge LoRA for inference.
- Shared-Adapter PRM (≈400M): reuse generator backbone; add LoRA adapters to 12 target layers and a calibration head. Lightweight gating network (~20M) to decide adapter path invocation.
- Sparse-MoE PRM (≈900M, 12 experts, 2 active/token): distilled from a 6B PRM on PRM800K + 60k synthetic Mixture-of-Thought traces.
- Baselines:
  1) Greedy 7B (T=0, top_p=1.0)
  2) Self-consistency (20 samples, T=0.7, top_p=0.95)
  3) 7B + 6B PRM (step-by-step verifier reranker)
  4) Self-Eval Guided Beam Search (generator self-critique reranker, k≤5)

4) Metrics
- Primary: final-answer accuracy; median and P95 GPU seconds/question; peak VRAM; mean tokens/output.
- Secondary: PRM usage stats (fraction of steps scored by Shared-Adapter only; fraction calling MoE); lazy-load overhead; step-level AUROC/F1 on PRM800K dev.

5) Environment and performance settings
- Libraries: transformers ≥4.41, peft ≥0.11, accelerate ≥0.30, bitsandbytes (optional), flash-attn 2 (optional), torch ≥2.2, pynvml, datasets, scikit-learn, torchmetrics.
- A100 80GB: fp16 autocast, FlashAttention-2, torch.compile(backend=inductor) if stable; attention kv_cache enabled; no gradient checkpointing (inference).
- RTX 4090 24GB: fp16 autocast; attention_slicing; FlashAttention-2 if supported; keep generator on GPU; Shared-Adapter PRM shares GPU backbone; MoE PRM weights on CPU pinned memory, lazy-loaded per call.
- Determinism: set all seeds; cudnn.deterministic=True; disable TF32 if needed for exact reproducibility.

6) Core implementation

6.1) Loading generator and adapters

6.2) Shared-Adapter PRM (reuse backbone + LoRA + gating + calibration)

Assume we trained and saved a PEFT LoRA config targeted to 12 layers plus a calibration head module. The gating network ingests a pooled representation of the sliding window hidden states and predicts use of the adapter path.

```python
from peft import PeftModel

PRM_ADAPTER_ID = os.environ.get("PRM_SHARED_ADAPTER_ID", "your-org/tinyprm-shared-adapter-lora")
CAL_HEAD_ID    = os.environ.get("PRM_CAL_HEAD_ID", "your-org/tinyprm-calibration-head")
GATE_ID        = os.environ.get("PRM_GATE_ID", "your-org/tinyprm-gating-mlp")

# Reuse the same backbone model weights (frozen); attach PRM LoRA
prm_shared = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    device_map={"": 0},
)
prm_shared.requires_grad_(False)
prm_shared = PeftModel.from_pretrained(prm_shared, PRM_ADAPTER_ID)
prm_shared.eval()

# Load gating net and calibration head (simple torch.nn.Module saved with state_dict)
class GatingMLP(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden=1024):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = torch.nn.Sequential(
            torch.nn.Linear(in_dim, hidden),
            torch.nn.ReLU(),
            torch.nn.Linear(hidden, 1),
            torch.nn.Sigmoid(),
        )
    def forward(self, feats):  # feats: [B, in_dim]
        return self.net(feats)

class CalibHead(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.head = torch.nn.Linear(in_dim, 1)
        self.temperature = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0))
    def forward(self, feats):
        logits = self.head(feats) / self.temperature.clamp(min=0.05, max=5.0)
        return torch.sigmoid(logits)

# Feature dimension equals hidden size of generator
d_model = prm_shared.config.hidden_size
gate = GatingMLP(in_dim=d_model).to(device).eval()
cal_head = CalibHead(in_dim=d_model).to(device).eval()

# Load weights
gate.load_state_dict(torch.load(f"{GATE_ID}.pt", map_location=device))
cal_head.load_state_dict(torch.load(f"{CAL_HEAD_ID}.pt", map_location=device))

@torch.no_grad()
def shared_adapter_prm_score(input_ids, attention_mask, window_mask=None):
    # window_mask: mask to select last W tokens for pooling; else use last token
    outputs = prm_shared.model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, output_hidden_states=True)
    hs = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [B, T, H]
    if window_mask is None:
        feats = hs[:, -1]  # [B, H]
    else:
        # masked average pooling over window
        wm = window_mask.float().unsqueeze(-1)  # [B, T, 1]
        feats = (hs * wm).sum(dim=1) / wm.sum(dim=1).clamp(min=1.0)
    # gating probability
    gprob = gate(feats).squeeze(-1)  # [B]
    # calibration head turns features into correctness probability
    p = cal_head(feats).squeeze(-1)  # [B]
    return p, gprob
```

6.3) Sparse-MoE PRM lazy-loading wrapper

We assume the MoE PRM is saved as a package with a small router kept resident on GPU and 12 expert submodules stored as separate safetensors files on CPU. Each call selects top-2 experts and pages them to GPU for a single forward, then offloads. We use pinned memory and synchronize timing.

```python
import safetensors.torch as sft

class MoEPRMRouter(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, num_experts=12):
        super().__init__()
        self.score = torch.nn.Linear(in_dim, num_experts)
    def forward(self, feats):
        logits = self.score(feats)  # [B, E]
        probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
        topk = torch.topk(probs, k=2, dim=-1)
        return topk.indices, topk.values

class MoEPRMWrapper:
    def __init__(self, base_model_id, router_ckpt, experts_dir, device="cuda"):
        self.device = device
        # Reuse backbone for feature extraction; keep on GPU
        self.backbone = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(base_model_id, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map={"": 0})
        self.backbone.eval()
        # Load router on GPU
        d_model = self.backbone.config.hidden_size
        self.router = MoEPRMRouter(d_model).to(device).eval()
        self.router.load_state_dict(torch.load(router_ckpt, map_location=device))
        self.experts_dir = experts_dir  # contains expert_0.safetensors ... expert_11.safetensors
        self._loaded = {}

    @contextmanager
    def _expert_ctx(self, expert_ids):
        # Load only required experts to GPU, pinned CPU transfer
        experts = {}
        start = time.perf_counter()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        for eid in expert_ids:
            pth = os.path.join(self.experts_dir, f"expert_{int(eid)}.safetensors")
            st = sft.load_file(pth, device=self.device)
            experts[int(eid)] = st  # assume this returns a torch.nn.Module-like or dict of params bound to a small head
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        load_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start)*1000
        try:
            yield experts, load_ms
        finally:
            # offload: delete and empty cache
            del experts
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    @torch.no_grad()
    def score(self, input_ids, attention_mask, window_mask=None):
        # Extract features via backbone
        outputs = self.backbone.model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, output_hidden_states=True)
        hs = outputs.hidden_states[-1]
        if window_mask is None:
            feats = hs[:, -1]
        else:
            wm = window_mask.float().unsqueeze(-1)
            feats = (hs * wm).sum(dim=1) / wm.sum(dim=1).clamp(min=1.0)
        # Route
        idx, _ = self.router(feats)  # [B, 2]
        uniq = torch.unique(idx)
        with self._expert_ctx(uniq.tolist()) as (experts, load_ms):
            # Combine expert scores (simple average or weighted, per distillation calibration)
            # Here we simulate expert heads as linear maps loaded from safetensors
            # Replace with your actual expert modules
            scores = []
            for b in range(feats.size(0)):
                e1, e2 = int(idx[b,0]), int(idx[b,1])
                # Suppose each expert is a dict with 'W' and 'b'
                def apply_expert(eid, x):
                    W = experts[eid]['W']  # [1, H]
                    b = experts[eid]['b']  # [1]
                    return torch.sigmoid((x * W).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + b)
                s1 = apply_expert(e1, feats[b:b+1])
                s2 = apply_expert(e2, feats[b:b+1])
                s = 0.5 * (s1 + s2)
                scores.append(s)
            p = torch.cat(scores, dim=0).squeeze(-1)  # [B]
            return p, float(load_ms)

# Instantiate MoE wrapper (router resident; experts lazy)
moe_prm = MoEPRMWrapper(MODEL_ID, router_ckpt="your-org/moe_router.pt", experts_dir="/path/to/moe_experts")
```

Note: The above expert scoring is a placeholder showing lazy-load and two-expert routing mechanics. In your implementation, each expert is a small MLP or head stack distilled from the 6B PRM. Save each expert as a small module state_dict and reconstruct it on the fly. Prefer Deepspeed-MoE/Tutel if available for training; at inference we intentionally avoid keeping all experts resident.

6.4) TinyPRM-Cascade controller and runners

```python
def logprob_gap(next_token_logits):
    # next_token_logits: [V]
    probs = F.log_softmax(next_token_logits, dim=-1)
    top2 = torch.topk(probs, k=2)
    return (top2.values[0] - top2.values[1]).item()

class TinyPRMCascade:
    def __init__(self, model, tokenizer, prm_shared, gate, cal_head, moe_prm=None,
                 pt_high=0.95, pt_low=0.65, dt_high=0.7, beam_k=5, horizon=12,
                 max_new_tokens=256, window_size=512, budget_multiplier=1.5,
                 device="cuda"):
        self.model = model
        self.tk = tokenizer
        self.shared = prm_shared
        self.gate = gate
        self.cal = cal_head
        self.moe = moe_prm
        self.pt_high = pt_high
        self.pt_low = pt_low
        self.dt_high = dt_high
        self.beam_k = beam_k
        self.horizon = horizon
        self.max_new_tokens = max_new_tokens
        self.window_size = window_size
        self.device = device
        self.stats = {}
        self.budget_multiplier = budget_multiplier

    @torch.no_grad()
    def run(self, prompt, greedy_time_estimate=None, global_budget_seconds=None):
        enc = self.tk(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(self.device)
        input_ids = enc.input_ids
        attn = enc.attention_mask
        start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        start.record()

        new_tokens = []
        prm_calls = 0
        moe_calls = 0
        lazy_overheads = []
        total_tokens = 0
        beams_spawned = 0

        # Estimate budget from greedy if provided
        if global_budget_seconds is None and greedy_time_estimate is not None:
            global_budget_seconds = self.budget_multiplier * greedy_time_estimate
        t0 = time.perf_counter()

        for step in range(self.max_new_tokens):
            # 1) forward to get next-token logits
            out = self.model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attn)
            next_logits = out.logits[:, -1, :]
            gap = logprob_gap(next_logits[0])
            # Greedy candidate
            greedy_token = torch.argmax(next_logits, dim=-1)

            # 2) Shared-Adapter PRM score on sliding window
            T = input_ids.size(1)
            win_len = min(self.window_size, T)
            window_mask = torch.zeros((1, T), device=self.device, dtype=torch.bool)
            window_mask[0, T-win_len:T] = True
            p_shared, gprob = shared_adapter_prm_score(input_ids, attn, window_mask)
            p = p_shared.item(); prm_calls += 1

            # 3) Adaptive decision
            elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
            budget_ok = True if global_budget_seconds is None else (elapsed < global_budget_seconds)
            if p > self.pt_high or gap > self.dt_high or not budget_ok:
                # Commit greedy
                next_id = greedy_token
            elif p > self.pt_low and self.moe is not None and budget_ok:
                # Spawn beams and rerank once by MoE PRM
                beams_spawned += 1
                beam_ids = []
                # Sample up to beam_k short rollouts
                for k in range(self.beam_k):
                    temp = 0.7; topp = 0.95
                    beam_input = input_ids.clone()
                    for h in range(self.horizon):
                        bo = self.model(beam_input, attention_mask=attn)
                        logits = bo.logits[:, -1, :]
                        probs = F.softmax(logits/temp, dim=-1)
                        if topp < 1.0:
                            sorted_probs, sorted_idx = torch.sort(probs, descending=True)
                            cum = torch.cumsum(sorted_probs, dim=-1)
                            cutoff = sorted_idx[cum > topp][0].item() if torch.any(cum > topp) else probs.size(-1)-1
                            mask = torch.ones_like(probs).bool()
                            mask[:, sorted_idx[:, cutoff+1:]] = False
                            probs = probs.masked_fill(~mask, 0.0)
                            probs = probs / probs.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
                        tok = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)
                        beam_input = torch.cat([beam_input, tok], dim=1)
                    beam_ids.append(beam_input)
                # Score beams with MoE PRM (single call)
                batch = torch.cat(beam_ids, dim=0)
                attn_beam = torch.ones_like(batch)
                p_moe, overhead_ms = self.moe.score(batch, attn_beam)
                moe_calls += 1
                lazy_overheads.append(overhead_ms)
                # Choose best beam's first token
                best = torch.argmax(p_moe).item()
                next_id = beam_ids[best][0, input_ids.shape[1]:input_ids.shape[1]+1]
            else:
                # Halt exploration and continue greedy
                next_id = greedy_token

            input_ids = torch.cat([input_ids, next_id.unsqueeze(0)], dim=1)
            attn = torch.ones_like(input_ids)
            new_tokens.append(next_id.item())
            total_tokens += 1

            # Heuristic stop: end-of-sequence or dataset-specific end token
            if next_id.item() == self.tk.eos_token_id:
                break

        end.record(); torch.cuda.synchronize()
        gpu_ms = start.elapsed_time(end)

        text = self.tk.decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True)
        return {
            "text": text,
            "gpu_seconds": gpu_ms / 1000.0,
            "tokens": total_tokens,
            "prm_calls": prm_calls,
            "moe_calls": moe_calls,
            "lazy_overhead_ms": lazy_overheads,
        }
```

```python
def compute_calibration_metrics(probs, labels):
    # Filter None labels
    x, y = np.array([p for p,l in zip(probs,labels) if l is not None]), np.array([l for p,l in zip(probs,labels) if l is not None])
    auroc = roc_auc_score(y, x)
    auprc = average_precision_score(y, x)
    brier = np.mean((x - y)**2)
    ece_metric = BinaryCalibrationError(n_bins=15, norm="l1").to("cpu")
    with torch.no_grad():
        ece = ece_metric(torch.tensor(x), torch.tensor(y)).item()
    return {"auroc": auroc, "auprc": auprc, "brier": brier, "ece": ece}
```

Experiment 3: Robustness and resource-constrained deployment with on-the-fly PRM loading

1) Goals and hypothesis
- Stress-test against adversarial distractions, 3× input length, and 5–10% poisoned retrieval, and verify compliance with ≤1.5× greedy median latency and ≤19 GB peak VRAM on RTX 4090 fp16.

2) Stressors and data perturbations
- BBH distraction: inject k irrelevant sentences into “navigate” and related tasks; verify no answer leakage.
- Long-input: prepend/append verbose but relevant context to achieve 3× input length; disable truncation.
- Noisy retrieval: interleave relevant with 5% (and 10% in ablation) poisoned facts; shuffle order.

3) Deployment harness and budgeting
- Generator always resident on GPU; Shared-Adapter PRM shares backbone; MoE router resident; experts lazy-loaded from CPU pinned memory per call.
- Budget controller enforces per-question wall-clock budget B = 1.5 × greedy_estimate; when exceeded, disallow MoE and reduce beams to 1.

```python
DISTRACTOR_POOL = load_dataset("ag_news", split="train")["text"]  # simple unrelated corpus

def inject_distractions(prompt, k=3, max_len=40):
    import random
    extras = [random.choice(DISTRACTOR_POOL) for _ in range(k)]
    extras = ["Note:"+e[:max_len] for e in extras]

def extend_with_context(prompt, multiplier=3):
    filler = "\n".join([prompt[:200]] * (multiplier-1))
    return filler + "\n" + prompt

def add_noisy_retrieval(prompt, relevant_passages, poison_passages, poison_rate=0.05):
    import random
    total = len(relevant_passages)
    n_poison = max(1, int(poison_rate*total))
    sample_poison = random.sample(poison_passages, n_poison)
    blocks = relevant_passages + sample_poison
    random.shuffle(blocks)
    ctx = "\n\n".join(blocks)
    return f"{ctx}\n\nQuestion:\n{prompt}"
```

5) Measurements and analysis

- PRM usage rates; MoE lazy-load overhead median and P95; total bytes transferred CPU↔GPU per question.
- Success criteria: accuracy drop <1–2% under 5% poison; <1% under 3× length; SC baseline degrades sharply under poison (≥9%). On 4090: median latency ≤1.5× greedy; peak VRAM ≤19 GB; MoE calls <20% steps; lazy-load overhead 3–5 ms median.


Training notes for PRMs (condensed, for completeness)

- Shared-Adapter PRM training
  - Initialize from generator; insert LoRA to 12 layers (rank 16–32) with PEFT. Freeze base; train LoRA + calibration head + gating MLP on PRM800K train with process supervision. Loss = focal KL (for calibration head) + BCE for gating signal derived from an uncertainty heuristic (e.g., step correctness entropy from teacher PRM or margin). Use AdamW, cosine decay, bf16/fp16 mixed precision, FlashAttention-2.
  - Validate on PRM800K dev; select checkpoint by AUROC and ECE.

- Sparse-MoE PRM distillation
  - Teacher: 6B PRM. Student: 12-expert MoE (total ~900M); route at token/window level to top-2 experts. Distill on PRM800K + 60k Mixture-of-Thought traces (CoT+PoT) with temperature T=2 logits matching and step-level BCE to gold when available. Use Tutel/DeepSpeed-MoE for training; export experts as separate modules for lazy inference.

- Calibration head with focal KL
  - Train a small head mapping hidden features to step correctness probability; loss: focal KL between predicted p and target q (teacher probabilities), with alpha/gamma tuned via grid search; post-hoc temperature scaling on a held-out set to tighten ECE.


Statistical testing and reporting templates

- Accuracy: paired McNemar test TinyPRM-Cascade vs baseline (same items). Report p-values and 95% CIs for difference in proportions (Agresti–Coull).
- Latency and tokens: paired bootstrap (10k resamples). Report mean difference and 95% BCa CI. Use median multipliers for headline.
- Calibration: AUROC 95% CI via DeLong bootstrap; ECE with bootstrap over items.


Ablations summary (spanning Exps 1–3 without duplication)
- Remove MoE (Exp 1 for Pareto; Exp 2 for calibration deltas) to quantify the refinement benefit.
- Remove adapter sharing (Exp 1 resource impact; Exp 3 VRAM/latency on 4090) to show memory blow-up without sharing.
- Freeze gating vs learned (Exp 2 compute allocation; Exp 3 budget clamp interactions).
- Beam budget/threshold sweeps (Exp 2 accuracy vs compute frontier; reuse best settings in Exp 1–3 main runs).
- Poison rates {0%, 5%, 10%} and length multipliers {1×, 2×, 3×} (Exp 3 robustness curves).


Reproducibility, logging, and safety

- Seeds fixed at 42 across Python/numpy/torch; deterministic flags set.
- JSONL per-example logs include: dataset, item id, prompt hash, thresholds, greedy_estimate, decisions (commit/branch/stop), PRM and MoE calls, lazy-load overheads, tokens, GPU seconds, peak VRAM snapshot, prediction, gold label.
- Cap max_new_tokens; enforce global PRM call caps per question (e.g., ≤20) to prevent runaway compute.
- Version-control config files for thresholds, beam budgets, and model ids; keep lockfile with library versions.


Expected outcomes summarized against success criteria

- Accuracy: +8% BBH, +5% GSM8K, +4% MATH over greedy; within ~1% of 7B+6B PRM.
- Latency/VRAM: median 1.35× greedy; peak VRAM ~19 GB vs ~34 GB for 6B PRM setup.
- Calibration: Shared-Adapter AUROC ~0.87 → MoE ~0.91; ECE ≤4% → ≤3%; Without adapters AUROC ~0.79.
- Robustness: <1% drop under 3× input; 1–2% under 5% poison; SC baseline drops ≥9% under poison.

This package of experiments isolates end-to-end Pareto efficiency (Exp 1), validates the PRMs’ calibration and early-commit quality (Exp 2), and demonstrates robustness and deployability under consumer-GPU constraints with on-the-fly PRM execution (Exp 3). The code scaffold is intentionally modular so you can plug in your actual checkpoints and run ablations without redundant pipelines.
